claims.evidence: Epilepsy Action: seizures classed as focal (one part of brain) or generalised (both sides).
Focal seizures: some people stay aware, for others awareness is affected; begins in one part of the brain.
claims.newSentence: Focal seizures start in one part of the brain, and some people stay aware during them while for others awareness is affected.

claims.evidence: Generalised = start in or very quickly affect both sides; 'does not usually stay conscious' not stated in retrieved text.
claims.newSentence: Generalised seizures start in, or very quickly affect, both sides of the brain.

claims.evidence: NHS inform: focal aware seizures are sometimes called warnings or auras.
Epilepsy Action: an aura is a type of focal seizure.
claims.newSentence: Epilepsy Action says an aura is a type of focal seizure in its own right.

claims.evidence: NHS symptoms page names rising stomach feeling, unusual smells/tastes, tingling; 'hard to describe' and 'events happened before' not retrieved.
claims.newSentence: Examples include a rising feeling in the tummy, unusual smells or tastes, and tingling in the arms and legs.

claims.evidence: Tonic phase: stiffening, loss of consciousness, usually falls.
Clonic phase: shaking/jerking follows stiffening.
Epilepsy Action: focal seizure can spread to both sides; focal to bilateral tonic-clonic.
Epilepsy Action: if the person did not go to hospital at the time, see a GP as soon as possible.
claims.newSentence: Epilepsy Action advises seeing a GP as soon as possible after a suspected seizure, even if the person did not go to hospital at the time.

claims.evidence: NICE: refer urgently so a specialist is involved early; QS211: seen within 2 weeks of presentation. 'Children over 2' and 'of the GP making the referral' not retrieved.
claims.newSentence: NICE says people with a suspected first seizure should be referred urgently so that a specialist is involved early in diagnosing epilepsy, and its quality standard aims for them to be seen within 2 weeks.

claims.evidence: 'GP may arrange tests while you wait' not retrieved; retrieved: NICE says 12-lead ECG after first suspected seizure; Epilepsy Action ECG to rule out heart problem.
claims.newSentence: Epilepsy Action says anyone with a suspected seizure should have an ECG, a heart tracing, to rule out a heart problem.

claims.evidence: Summary of Epilepsy Action diagnosis page: no single test confirms epilepsy (blended summary; moderate confidence).
NICE: if EEG requested after first seizure, do as soon as possible.
Normal EEG not excluding epilepsy supported (NICE); 'positive finding supports provisional diagnosis' not retrieved.
claims.newSentence: A normal EEG does not rule epilepsy out, because many people with epilepsy do not show abnormal activity between seizures.

claims.evidence: NICE: offer MRI to people diagnosed with epilepsy except IGE and SeLECTS.
Retrieved: one source says MRI cannot determine by itself whether someone has epilepsy, useful alongside other information; 'help clinician judge likely cause' overreach.
claims.newSentence: An MRI scan cannot decide on its own whether someone has epilepsy and is useful alongside other information.

claims.evidence: Epilepsy Action recommends a seizure diary and bringing it to appointments.
claims.newSentence: Epilepsy Action advises keeping a seizure diary and taking it to appointments.

claims.evidence: Referral to specialist epilepsy centre when unclear not retrieved.
NHS inform: diagnosis can still be made from the description of seizures even when tests show nothing (added sentence).
claims.newSentence: NHS inform says a diagnosis can still be made from the person's description of their seizures even when tests show nothing.

claims.evidence: NHS England treatment page: medicine to prevent seizures (anti-seizure) is the main treatment.
claims.newSentence: The NHS says medicine to prevent seizures, called anti-seizure medicine, is the main treatment for epilepsy.

claims.evidence: NHS 111 Wales: help control seizures in about 7 out of 10 people (NICE says about two-thirds); nhs.uk page itself lacked the figure.
claims.newSentence: NHS 111 Wales says these medicines help control seizures in about 7 out of 10 people.

claims.evidence: NHS England: medicines do not cure epilepsy but can stop seizures.
NHS inform: some ASMs reduce effectiveness of some contraception; 'combined pill and implants' not retrieved; 'worth raising with a doctor' is an instruction.
claims.newSentence: NHS inform says some anti-seizure medicines can reduce how well some types of contraception work.

claims.evidence: Surgery considered only if medication not working; VNS when medicines failed.
'Only a minority of people with hard-to-control epilepsy' not retrieved; NHS England says surgery is for rare cases.
claims.newSentence: The NHS describes surgery as an option for rare cases.

claims.evidence: NICE evidence review: VNS for people whose seizures not controlled by ASMs and not suitable for surgery.
claims.newSentence: NICE's evidence review describes vagus nerve stimulation as used for people whose seizures have not responded to anti-seizure medicines and who are not suitable for surgery.

claims.evidence: NHS: ketogenic diet high fat, low carbohydrate/protein, mainly used in children; Chelsea and Westminster: usually reserved for children who have not responded to medicines.
claims.newSentence: The ketogenic diet, which is high in fat and low in carbohydrate and protein, is mainly used in children, usually those who have not responded to medicines.

claims.evidence: NHS inform: for children only under supervision of an epilepsy specialist with a dietitian.
claims.newSentence: NHS inform says it should only be used under the supervision of an epilepsy specialist with the help of a dietitian.

claims.evidence: Added: NHS England says discuss treatment with a specialist if there is a chance of becoming pregnant while taking epilepsy medicine.
claims.newSentence: The NHS says it is very important to discuss treatment with a specialist if there is a chance of becoming pregnant while taking epilepsy medicine.

claims.evidence: NHS Healthier Together: cushion or gently hold the head; 'support gently' and 'not try to move them' not retrieved.
claims.newSentence: NHS advice for a convulsive seizure is to cushion or gently hold the person's head to protect it from injury.

claims.evidence: Retrieved: do not restrain, do not put anything in mouth; 'unless in immediate danger' not retrieved.
claims.newSentence: The NHS also advises not restraining the person and not putting anything in their mouth.

claims.evidence: Retrieved: once jerking stops turn person onto side (recovery position); 'stay with them and note times' not retrieved.
claims.newSentence: Once the jerking stops, the advice is to turn the person onto their side in the recovery position.

claims.evidence: NHS symptoms page: call 999 if first time, longer than usual for them, or longer than 5 minutes if usual length not known.
NHS: call 999 if does not recover as usual or has another seizure before recovering; serious injury/breathing problems (summary); 'full consciousness' wording not retrieved.
claims.newSentence: A 999 call is also advised if the person does not recover as usual, has another seizure before recovering, is seriously injured or has trouble breathing.

claims.evidence: CDC defines status epilepticus (over 5 minutes or back-to-back seizures); NHS inform says phone 999 immediately if suspected; draft attributed the definition to NHS inform.
claims.newSentence: Status epilepticus, a seizure lasting more than 5 minutes or seizures back to back with no recovery in between, needs emergency treatment, and NHS inform says to phone 999 straight away if it is suspected.

claims.evidence: Added: Epilepsy Action first aid leaflet says clear the area of anything potentially harmful.
claims.newSentence: Epilepsy Action adds that anything potentially harmful nearby should be cleared.

claims.evidence: NHS 111 Wales suggests a seizure diary; triggers listed by Epilepsy Action/Epilepsy Society/CDC, not 'NHS suggests'; 'food' not retrieved (alcohol is).
claims.newSentence: NHS 111 Wales suggests keeping a seizure diary, noting when seizures happen and what the person was doing beforehand, to help work out triggers.

claims.evidence: Not 'Epilepsy Action' specifically; Epilepsy Society and NHS-linked guidance list lack of sleep, missed medicine, stress, alcohol; CDC lists period hormones.
claims.newSentence: Epilepsy charities and NHS guidance list lack of sleep, missing anti-seizure medicine, stress and alcohol among possible triggers, and the CDC lists hormonal changes with a period.

claims.evidence: Exercise, yoga and meditation as help: not found in any result.
GOV.UK: must stop driving and tell DVLA after any epileptic seizure; NHS wording not retrieved.
claims.newSentence: GOV.UK says a person must stop driving straight away after any epileptic seizure and tell the DVLA.

claims.evidence: GOV.UK: reapplying depends on seizure type and time seizure-free.
claims.newSentence: When driving can start again depends on the type of seizure and how long the person has been seizure-free.

claims.evidence: Contraception and pregnancy planning supported (NHS England); jobs not retrieved; swimming advice was child-specific.
claims.newSentence: Epilepsy can also affect decisions about contraception and planning a pregnancy.

claims.evidence: NHS: 'An epileptic seizure usually stops by itself and does not cause any lasting problems'; 'for most people' not in source.
claims.newSentence: The NHS says an epileptic seizure usually stops by itself and does not cause any lasting problems.

claims.evidence: NHS: rarely a seizure lasts long or several without recovery (status epilepticus, urgent); small SUDEP risk; 'injury' as main risk not retrieved.
claims.newSentence: Rarely, a seizure can last a long time, or several can happen without recovery in between, which is called status epilepticus and is a medical emergency that needs a 999 call.

claims.evidence: NHS: small risk of SUDEP, but rare, and treatment can reduce risk.
claims.newSentence: There is also a small risk of sudden unexpected death in epilepsy (SUDEP). The NHS describes SUDEP as rare and says epilepsy treatment can reduce the risk.

claims.evidence: CDC lists uncontrolled or frequent seizures among SUDEP risk factors; 'which is why seizure control matters' is inference.
claims.newSentence: The CDC lists frequent or uncontrolled seizures among the factors linked to a higher risk.

claims.evidence: Epilepsy Action: not enough research to prove pillows reduce SUDEP risk (not 'no research evidence').
claims.newSentence: Epilepsy Action says there is not enough research to show that anti-suffocation pillows reduce the risk.

claims.evidence: Added: Epilepsy Action says 3 to 5 in 100 people with epilepsy have photosensitive seizures; worded as a small number.
claims.newSentence: Flashing lights trigger seizures in a small number of people.

claims.evidence: NHS: ASMs do not cure but can stop seizures.
NHS 111 Wales: about 7 out of 10.
claims.newSentence: NHS 111 Wales says they help control seizures in about 7 out of 10 people.
